label: Person
name: Abbé de Coulmier
summary:
François Simonet de Coulmier (1741–1818), known as the Abbé de Coulmier, was a French Catholic priest and theatre director who became famous as the administrator of the Charenton asylum near Paris and for his extraordinarily permissive treatment of its most notorious patient — the Marquis de Sade. Born into a noble family and ordained a priest, he was elected to the Estates-General in 1789 as a representative of the clergy.

Coulmier was appointed director of Charenton in 1797 and ran it on unusually humane principles, allowing patients significant freedoms. His most controversial decision was to permit the Marquis de Sade — imprisoned for his scandalous writings — to stage theatrical productions at Charenton using patients as actors, with wealthy Parisians admitted as audience. These performances attracted considerable fashionable attention until they were shut down by Napoleon's government in 1813.

Coulmier's relationship with Sade, his theatrical patronage of the asylum, and his own complicated position as a priest who had survived both the ancien régime and the Revolution have made him a fascinating marginal figure in French cultural history. Peter Weiss's 1963 play 'The Persecution and Assassination of Jean-Paul Marat as Performed by the Inmates of the Asylum of Charenton Under the Direction of the Marquis de Sade' (Marat/Sade) portrays Coulmier as a nervous bourgeois administrator — a portrayal that made him known to twentieth-century theatre audiences worldwide.
